newsitem.title: BELGIUM: UIP, EU settle dispute over pay-TV film rights.
newsitem.headline: UIP, EU settle dispute over pay-TV film rights.

text.p: UIP, Hollywood's distribution arm, said on Friday it had settled a dispute with the European Commission over the licensing of pay-television film rights in the European Union.

The agreement foresees that United International Pictures's parent companies, Paramount, Universal and MGM, will in the future sell their rights directly to pay-TV channels rather than through UIP Pay Television, it said in a statement.

"UIP Pay Television is pleased to have reached this resolution with the European Commission. It ends a protracted and complex set of proceedings, is consistent with the studios' business practices, and meets the ongoing objectives of both the studios and EU competition policy," it said.
A Commission spokesman confirmed the deal, but was unable to elaborate.

The pay-TV rights issue is separate from a more controversial investigation into UIP's rules on the distribution of films to European cinemas which culminated last summer with Commission raids on the premises of UIP in London, Paris and Brussels last July.
Both the spokesman and UIP's executive vice-president Brian Reilly could give no indication of when the second dispute may be settled.
In June 1993 UIP asked the Commission to renew a 1988 five-year exemption to competition rules allowing it to effectively distribute in Europe the films of the three studios.
Reilly hoped for an equally satisfactory agreement.

"We remain very confident that when the Commission concludes its investigation...that we have satisfied the conditions for a renewal of the exemption," he told Reuters on the telephone from London. He argued there had been no "material changes" that would justify the Commission modifying its position.
UIP has long been accused by its European rivals of operating a "block booking" system, forcing cinemas to buy film packages to get Hollywood blockbusters. UIP has denied the accusations.

Reilly declined to say what the Commission inspectors were looking for during its raids or what documents it had taken away. The Commission was equally discreet as is usually the case in antitrust probes.
Reilly said the Commission had not sent it a so-called statement of objections, a key step in investigation proceedings which normally detail the Commission's grievances.
But UIP had continued to cooperate with the Commission since July, replying to its requests for information, he said.

Following the pay-TV film rights deal, UIP will discuss with its customers in the next 18 months what to do with existing licensing agreements -- whether they want them to be administered by UIP or the film companies.

Paramount is a unit of Germany's Viacom, Universal is ultimately controlled by Canadian beverages company Seagram and MGM was sold last July by Credit Lyonnais to a group led by U.S. billionaire Kirk Kerkorian and Australia's Seven Network Ltd which is partly owned by Rupert Murdoch.
